claim: The Synapsin iBioID proteome identified 200 proteins selectively enriched in presynaptic terminals.
source: This resulted in a network of 200 proteins selectively enriched in presynaptic terminals (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by the mass spectrometry data and filtering criteria described in the manuscript, which identified 200 proteins enriched in the BioID2-Synapsin samples compared to controls.

claim: The Synapsin iBioID proteome is highly enriched for proteins implicated in presynaptic function.
source: Bioinformatic network analysis revealed that the Synapsin iBioID proteome is highly enriched for proteins implicated in presynaptic function (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis showing enrichment of known presynaptic proteins and functional categories related to presynaptic processes.

claim: The Synapsin iBioID proteome contains proteins from synaptic vesicles (20 proteins), active zones (8 proteins), and recycling endosomes (6 proteins).
source: Multiple compartments of presynaptic terminals were represented, including synaptic vesicles (20 proteins), active zones (eight proteins), and recycling endosomes (six proteins).
evidence: The claim is supported by the identification and categorization of proteins in the mass spectrometry data.

claim: The Synapsin iBioID proteome covers both excitatory and inhibitory terminals.
source: The proteome covered both excitatory and inhibitory terminals, as suggested by the identification of Slc17a6 (Vglut2), Slc1a2 (Glt1), Slc32a1 (Vgat), and Gad2.
evidence: The claim is supported by the identification of specific marker proteins for excitatory and inhibitory synapses in the proteome.

claim: The Synapsin iBioID proteome is significantly enriched for the biological process of 'synaptic vesicle endocytosis' (22 proteins, p=1.7x10−6).
source: DAVID analysis (Dennis et al., 2003) of the proteome found a significant enrichment for the biological processes of 'synaptic vesicle endocytosis' (22 proteins, p=1.7x10−6)
evidence: The claim is supported by DAVID bioinformatics analysis of the proteome data.

claim: The Synapsin iBioID proteome is significantly enriched for the biological process of 'synaptic vesicle exocytosis' (30 proteins, p=3.6x10−9).
source: DAVID analysis (Dennis et al., 2003) of the proteome found a significant enrichment for the biological processes of 'synaptic vesicle endocytosis' (22 proteins, p=1.7x10−6) and 'synaptic vesicle exocytosis' (30 proteins, p=3.6x10−9), among others.
evidence: The claim is supported by DAVID bioinformatics analysis of the proteome data.

claim: Regulators of the actin cytoskeleton were heavily overrepresented in the Synapsin iBioID proteome (54 proteins, p=9.8x10−7).
source: Regulators of the actin cytoskeleton were heavily overrepresented in the Synapsin iBioID proteome (54 proteins, p=9.8x10−7).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the proteome data showing significant enrichment of actin regulators.

claim: Very few actin signaling molecules in the Synapsin iBioID proteome had been previously studied in presynaptic terminals.
source: Importantly, very few of these actin signaling molecules had been previously studied in presynaptic terminals (Figure 1E, 'Actin cytoskeleton' vs 'Known presynaptic').
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the identified proteins with literature on known presynaptic proteins.

claim: 54% of proteins (108 proteins) in the Synapsin iBioID network were previously known to be presynaptic.
source: Overall, the network was highly interconnected with 54% of proteins (108 proteins) previously known to be presynaptic, suggesting high coverage of the presynaptic compartment.
evidence: The claim is based on literature review and annotation of the identified proteins.

claim: 14 out of 23 candidate genes from the Synapsin iBioID proteome displayed robust endogenous protein localization to presynaptic terminals when tagged using HiUGE.
source: Positive labeling was observed from 19 out of 23 genes, of which 14 displayed a robust signal with good signal-to-noise ratio above background fluorescence (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data from HiUGE-tagged proteins.

claim: All 14 validated candidate proteins from the Synapsin iBioID proteome were significantly enriched in presynaptic terminals compared to a GFP cell fill.
source: All endogenous candidate proteins were expressed throughout the cell body, dendrites, and in some cases dendritic spines (Figure 2C–P). As expected, all 14 proteins were also expressed in axons, with significant enrichment in presynaptic terminals as compared to a GFP cell fill (Figure 2B,Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunocytochemistry data showing presynaptic enrichment.

claim: Regulators of Arp2/3 were significantly enriched in the Synapsin iBioID network.
source: Using overrepresentation analysis, we found that regulators of Arp2/3, including Rac1, were significantly enriched in the Synapsin iBioID network (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical overrepresentation analysis of the proteome data.

claim: Regulators of formins were not significantly enriched in the Synapsin iBioID network.
source: In contrast, regulators of formins, which nucleate linear actin filaments (Schönichen and Geyer, 2010), were not significantly enriched.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical overrepresentation analysis of the proteome data.

claim: The majority of synaptic Rac1 labeling (70.3%) localized to presynaptic terminals in hippocampal CA1 of young adult mice.
source: However, unexpectedly, the majority of synaptic Rac1 labeling (70.3%) localized to presynaptic terminals, with 49.6% of presynaptic labeling adjacent to synaptic vesicle membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: 49.6% of presynaptic Rac1 labeling was adjacent to synaptic vesicle membranes in hippocampal CA1 of young adult mice.
source: However, unexpectedly, the majority of synaptic Rac1 labeling (70.3%) localized to presynaptic terminals, with 49.6% of presynaptic labeling adjacent to synaptic vesicle membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 gold particles were located on plasma membranes (44.1%) and occasionally on mitochondrial membranes (6.3%).
source: Presynaptic gold particles coding for Rac1 were also located on plasma membranes (44.1%) and occasionally on mitochondrial membranes (6.3%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 was positioned similarly to synaptic vesicles (mean distance ± SD, 176 ± 155 nm for Rac1, and 172 ± 108 nm for synaptic vesicles).
source: Overall, presynaptic Rac1 was positioned similarly to synaptic vesicles (mean distance ± SD, 176 ± 155 nm for Rac1, and 172 ± 108 nm for synaptic vesicles).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: ArpC2 was concentrated in dendritic spines approximately 200 nm below the PSD.
source: As reported previously (Rácz and Weinberg, 2008), ArpC2 was concentrated in dendritic spines approximately 200 nm below the PSD (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy data and cites previous work.

claim: A fraction of ArpC2 gold particles (~27%) localized to presynaptic terminals.
source: However, a fraction of gold particles (~27%) localized to presynaptic terminals with a consistent and specific distribution.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: ArpC2 was overlapping with synaptic vesicles, but also localized to the presynaptic area beyond the synaptic vesicle cluster, away from the active zone (mean distance ± SD, 298 ± 159 nm for ArpC2, and 173 ± 129 nm for synaptic vesicles).
source: ArpC2 was overlapping with synaptic vesicles, but it also localized to the presynaptic area beyond the synaptic vesicle cluster, away from the active zone (mean distance ± SD, 298 ± 159 nm for ArpC2, and 173 ± 129 nm for synaptic vesicles).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect the amplitude, charge transfer, or kinetics of single evoked EPSCs.
source: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect the amplitude, charge transfer, or kinetics of single evoked EPSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect the paired pulse ratio (PPR) of EPSCs.
source: It also did not affect the paired pulse ratio (PPR) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect the amplitude or frequency of strontium-induced quantal events.
source: Here, presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect the amplitude or frequency of strontium-induced quantal events (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion reduced short-term synaptic depression in response to high-frequency stimulation at excitatory synapses.
source: Surprisingly, presynaptic Rac1 deletion reduced short-term synaptic depression in response to HFS (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures showing altered responses to 20 Hz stimulation trains.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion increased the synaptic vesicle replenishment rate at excitatory synapses without altering release probability or RRP size.
source: Quantification of the cumulative EPSC curve showed that presynaptic Rac1 deletion increased the synaptic vesicle replenishment rate, without altering release probability or RRP size.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cumulative EPSC curves from electrophysiology data.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect single evoked IPSCs, PPR, or quantal events at inhibitory synapses.
source: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion from inhibitory neurons caused similar effects as in excitatory neurons; there were no effects on single evoked IPSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G), PPR (Figure 4F), quantal events (Figure 4G), or asynchronous release during HFS trains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion reduced short-term depression of IPSCs due to an increase in the synaptic vesicle replenishment rate at inhibitory synapses.
source: However, there was a reduction in the short-term depression of IPSCs due to an increase in the synaptic vesicle replenishment rate (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Rac1 negatively regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Together, these data show that Rac1 negatively regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, suggesting that this is a common function of Rac1 across different kinds of presynaptic terminals.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data showing similar effects of Rac1 deletion at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion in excitatory neurons increased the amplitude, charge, and decay time constants of single evoked EPSCs.
source: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion in excitatory neurons increased the amplitude, charge, and decay time constants of single evoked EPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion decreased PPR across interstimulus intervals at excitatory synapses.
source: It also decreased PPR across interstimulus intervals (Figure 5C), suggesting an increased release probability.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion did not affect quantal amplitude, but significantly increased the frequency of quantal events at excitatory synapses.
source: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion did not affect quantal amplitude, but it significantly increased the frequency of quantal events (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion did not affect the density of synapses formed by axons.
source: Since Arpc3 deletion did not affect the density of synapses formed by axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), the frequency effect was likely due to increased release probability rather than increased synapse number.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data quantifying synapse density along axons.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion reduced short-term synaptic depression in response to 20 Hz light stimulation at excitatory synapses.
source: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion also reduced short-term synaptic depression in response to 20 Hz light stimulation (Figure 5E), with no significant change in asynchronous release during the train (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion increased both release probability and synaptic vesicle replenishment rate at excitatory synapses.
source: Quantification of the cumulative EPSC showed that there was an increase in both release probability and synaptic vesicle replenishment rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cumulative EPSC curves from electrophysiology data.

claim: The same phenotypes observed at excitatory synapses were observed by Arpc3 deletion in presynaptic inhibitory neurons.
source: The same phenotypes were observed by Arpc3 deletion in presynaptic inhibitory neurons (Figure 5F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Both Rac1 and Arpc3 WT and KO neurons were able to consistently fire light-evoked action potentials at 20 Hz.
source: Importantly for these experiments, both Rac1 and Arpc3 WT and KO neurons were able to consistently fire light-evoked action potentials at 20 Hz (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B,F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Rac1 deletion increased synaptic vesicle replenishment rate without affecting the action potential waveform or release probability.
source: Rac1 deletion increased synaptic vesicle replenishment rate without affecting the action potential waveform (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–E) or release probability.
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings and electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Arpc3 deletion did not affect most intrinsic properties of neurons, but it did increase the width of light-evoked action potentials.
source: Arpc3 deletion did not affect most intrinsic properties of neurons, but it did increase the width of light-evoked action potentials (Figure 5—figure supplement 3H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Arpc3 deletion increased the width of action potentials from current injection, suggesting a change in intrinsic membrane properties.
source: It also increased the width of action potentials from current injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 3J), suggesting there was a change in intrinsic membrane properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 inhibition did not alter baseline synaptic transmission or PPR at excitatory synapses.
source: Similar to the genetic knockout, presynaptic Rac1 inhibition did not alter baseline synaptic transmission or PPR, with electrically evoked EPSCs having normal decay kinetics with a time constant ~4.5 ms (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 inhibition had no effect on quantal release parameters, as measured by mEPSCs recorded in the presence of TTX.
source: There was also no effect on quantal release parameters, as measured by mEPSCs recorded in the presence of TTX (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 inhibition reduced short-term depression at both 20 Hz and 40 Hz due to an increased synaptic vesicle replenishment rate, with no change in RRP size or release probability at excitatory synapses.
source: Electrical stimulation at both 20 Hz and 40 Hz showed that presynaptic Rac1 inhibition reduced short-term depression due to an increased synaptic vesicle replenishment rate, with no change in RRP size or release probability (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide.

claim: Hyperosmotic shock with 500 mM sucrose confirmed there was no difference in RRP size between control and Rac1 inhibition conditions at excitatory synapses.
source: Finally, hyperosmotic shock with 500 mM sucrose confirmed there was no difference in RRP size (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 inhibition had similar phenotypes at inhibitory synapses as at excitatory synapses.
source: These phenotypes were similar at inhibitory synapses (Figure 6F–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide.

claim: Rac1 negatively regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment by acting specifically at presynaptic terminals, and near synaptic vesicles.
source: Together, these data show that Rac1 negatively regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment by acting specifically at presynaptic terminals, and near synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data from experiments using the spatially restricted Rac1 inhibitory peptide.

claim: In presynaptic Arpc3 WT neurons, presynaptic Rac1 inhibition increased vesicle replenishment rate at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: As expected, in presynaptic Arpc3 WT neurons, presynaptic Rac1 inhibition increased vesicle replenishment rate at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Figure 7C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide in Arpc3 WT neurons.

claim: In presynaptic Arpc3 KO neurons expressing the scrambled control, the vesicle replenishment rate was increased.
source: In presynaptic Arpc3 KO neurons expressing the scrambled control, the vesicle replenishment rate was similarly increased, also as expected (Figure 7D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures expressing the scrambled control peptide in Arpc3 KO neurons.

claim: In presynaptic Arpc3 KO neurons expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide, there was no additional increase in the vesicle replenishment rate.
source: However, in presynaptic Arpc3 KO neurons expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide, there was no additional increase in the vesicle replenishment rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures expressing the Rac1 inhibitory peptide in Arpc3 KO neurons.

claim: The occlusion of Rac1 inhibition effects in Arpc3 KO neurons shows that Arp2/3, and thus actin remodeling, is likely required for Rac1 to alter synaptic vesicle replenishment in presynaptic terminals.
source: This occlusion shows that Arp2/3, and thus actin remodeling, is likely required for Rac1 to alter synaptic vesicle replenishment in presynaptic terminals.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data showing occlusion of Rac1 inhibition effects in Arpc3 KO neurons.

claim: Acute inactivation of presynaptic Rac1 signaling using PA-Rac1 DN resulted in reduced short-term synaptic depression due to an increase in synaptic vesicle replenishment rate.
source: Acute inactivation of presynaptic Rac1 signaling phenocopied both the genetic Rac1 deletion and the spatially restricted peptide-based Rac1 inhibition; presynaptic stimulation of PA-Rac1 DN resulted in reduced short-term synaptic depression due to an increase in synaptic vesicle replenishment rate (Figure 8D,F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing PA-Rac1 DN.

claim: Acute activation of Rac1 signaling using PA-Rac1 CA resulted in increased short-term synaptic depression due to a decrease in synaptic vesicle replenishment rate.
source: Conversely, acute activation of Rac1 signaling drove the phenotype in the opposite direction. Presynaptic stimulation of PA-Rac1 CA resulted in increased short-term synaptic depression due to a decrease in synaptic vesicle replenishment rate (Figure 8E,F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing PA-Rac1 CA.

claim: Neither PA-Rac1 DN nor PA-Rac1 CA manipulation affected release probability or RRP size.
source: Neither manipulation affected release probability or RRP size.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from hippocampal cultures expressing PA-Rac1 constructs.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 signaling sets the precise level of synaptic depression through its negative regulation of vesicle replenishment.
source: This bidirectional effect demonstrates that presynaptic Rac1 signaling sets the precise level of synaptic depression through its negative regulation of vesicle replenishment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data showing bidirectional control of synaptic depression by PA-Rac1 manipulation.

claim: Rac1 activity was significantly elevated in presynaptic boutons upon electrical stimulation to induce action potential trains.
source: Upon electrical stimulation to induce action potential trains, Rac1 activity was significantly elevated in presynaptic boutons (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2pFLIM data from organotypic hippocampal slices expressing the Rac1 activity sensor.

claim: The increase in Rac1 activity in presynaptic boutons was persistent for a period of 60–90 s.
source: Interestingly, this increase in activity was persistent for a period of 60–90 s, as measured by an increase in binding fraction.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2pFLIM data from organotypic hippocampal slices expressing the Rac1 activity sensor.

claim: There was no change in Rac1 binding fraction in the presence of TTX.
source: There was no change in binding fraction in the presence of TTX (Figure 9F–G), confirming that presynaptic Rac1 activation is action potential-dependent.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2pFLIM data from organotypic hippocampal slices expressing the Rac1 activity sensor in the presence of TTX.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 activation is action potential-dependent.
source: There was no change in binding fraction in the presence of TTX (Figure 9F–G), confirming that presynaptic Rac1 activation is action potential-dependent.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the 2pFLIM data showing no change in Rac1 activity in the presence of TTX.

claim: There was no change in Rac1 binding fraction in the presence of Cd2+.
source: There was also no change in binding fraction in the presence of Cd2+ (Figure 9H–I), demonstrating that presynaptic Rac1 activation requires calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2pFLIM data from organotypic hippocampal slices expressing the Rac1 activity sensor in the presence of Cd2+.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 activation requires calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: There was also no change in binding fraction in the presence of Cd2+ (Figure 9H–I), demonstrating that presynaptic Rac1 activation requires calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the 2pFLIM data showing no change in Rac1 activity in the presence of Cd2+.

claim: Nearly all (~92%) of boutons from GFP+ mCherry+ axons contained synapsin.
source: Post-hoc staining of slices revealed that nearly all (~92%) of boutons from GFP+ mCherry+ axons contained synapsin (identified by local axonal swelling, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), showing that these boutons tightly corresponded to presynaptic terminals.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from organotypic hippocampal slices expressing the Rac1 activity sensor.

claim: A high-frequency train of action potentials leads to the activation of Rac1 in presynaptic terminals through calcium signaling.
source: In summary, these data demonstrate a high-frequency train of action potentials leads to the activation of Rac1 in presynaptic terminals through calcium signaling.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the 2pFLIM data showing Rac1 activation in response to electrical stimulation that is blocked by TTX and Cd2+.

claim: The time scale of Rac1 activity observed, on the order of tens of seconds, supports its physiological role in presynaptic plasticity.
source: The time scale of Rac1 activity observed, on the order of tens of seconds, further supports its physiological role in presynaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the 2pFLIM data showing the time course of Rac1 activation.

claim: BioID2-Synapsin was enriched in presynaptic boutons similarly to Bassoon, an active zone marker.
source: BioID2-Synapsin was enriched in presynaptic boutons similarly to Bassoon, an active zone marker, while the localization of BioID2 was indistinguishable from GFP, confirming it acts as a soluble fill (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data from cultured hippocampal neurons expressing BioID2-Synapsin.

claim: The biotinylation activity of BioID2-Synapsin was significantly enhanced in presynaptic terminals in comparison to BioID2 alone.
source: The biotinylation activity of BioID2-Synapsin was also significantly enhanced in presynaptic terminals in comparison to BioID2 alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data from cultured hippocampal neurons expressing BioID2-Synapsin.

claim: Only Rac1 was significantly enriched among Rho GTPases in the Synapsin iBioID proteome.
source: Most interestingly, at the level of Rho GTPase signaling, only Rac1 was significantly enriched.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data from the Synapsin iBioID proteome.

claim: Several Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factors (GEFs: Trio, Itsn1, and Itsn2) and GTPase Activating Proteins (GAPs: Bcr, Arhgap1, Arhgap32, and Arhgap44) were identified in the Synapsin iBioID proteome.
source: We also identified several Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factors (GEFs: Trio, Itsn1, and Itsn2) and GTPase Activating Proteins (GAPs: Bcr, Arhgap1, Arhgap32, and Arhgap44), which activate and inactivate Rho GTPases, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data from the Synapsin iBioID proteome.

claim: Downstream of Rac1, the Synapsin iBioID proteome identified its effector proteins Pak1, Cttn, and members of the WAVE complex (Cyfip2 and Abi2).
source: Downstream of Rac1, we identified its effector proteins Pak1, Cttn, and members of the WAVE complex (Cyfip2 and Abi2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data from the Synapsin iBioID proteome.

claim: Cortactin and WAVE are nucleation promoting factors that activate the Arp2/3 complex to nucleate branched actin filaments.
source: Cortactin and WAVE are nucleation promoting factors that activate the Arp2/3 complex to nucleate branched actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the function of cortactin and WAVE.

claim: Rac1 localized to the PSD, which is consistent with its known function in dendritic spine development and plasticity.
source: Rac1 localized to the PSD (Figure 3E), which is consistent with its known function in dendritic spine development and plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy data and cites established knowledge about Rac1 function.

claim: The overlapping distributions of Rac1 and Arp2/3 at synaptic vesicles suggest a potential common presynaptic function related to synaptic vesicle modulation.
source: Taken together, the overlapping distributions of Rac1 and Arp2/3 at synaptic vesicles suggest a potential common presynaptic function related to synaptic vesicle modulation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the immunogold electron microscopy data showing overlapping distributions of Rac1 and Arp2/3.

claim: Loss of Rac1 is not expected until after synaptic maturation in the mixed culture system, assuming ~24 hr for Cre expression to begin and ~72 hr for turnover of the endogenous protein.
source: To minimize developmental effects, AAV-hSyn-Cre was added after 10 days in vitro (DIV10) to half the coverslips, deleting Rac1 from neurons expressing ChR2 (Figure 4B). In this system, loss of Rac1 is not expected until after synaptic maturation, assuming ~24 hr for Cre expression to begin and ~72 hr for turnover of the endogenous protein.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design and assumptions about the timing of Cre-mediated recombination and protein turnover.

claim: There was no effect of late Rac1 deletion on presynaptic neuron viability.
source: There was no effect of this late Rac1 deletion on presynaptic neuron viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of the number of presynaptic neurons per coverslip.

claim: In the mixed culture system, recorded responses were from the activation of ~10 presynaptic excitatory neurons or ~eight presynaptic inhibitory neurons for a given target neuron.
source: Based on the sparse seeding of ChR2 neurons and previously reported connection probabilities in hippocampal cultures (Amendola et al., 2015; Barral and D Reyes, 2016; Gerkin et al., 2013; Ivenshitz and Segal, 2010; Papa et al., 1995; Shimazaki et al., 2015; Soriano et al., 2008), we estimated that for a given target neuron, recorded responses were from the activation of ~10 presynaptic excitatory neurons or ~eight presynaptic inhibitory neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using CaMPARI2 data and previously reported connection probabilities.

claim: 20 Hz light stimulation for 2 s in 2 mM Ca2+ is sufficient to exhaust the RRP in the mixed culture system.
source: Thus, in this system, 20 Hz light stimulation for 2 s in 2 mM Ca2+ is sufficient to exhaust the RRP and estimate its size.
evidence: The claim is based on validation experiments comparing responses in 2 mM and 4 mM Ca2+ and comparing optical and electrical stimulation.

claim: Presynaptic Rac1 deletion did not affect asynchronous release during the train, as measured by the steady-state basal current.
source: There was no effect on asynchronous release during the train, as measured by the steady-state basal current (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion did not affect asynchronous release during HFS trains at excitatory synapses.
source: Presynaptic Arpc3 deletion also reduced short-term synaptic depression in response to 20 Hz light stimulation (Figure 5E), with no significant change in asynchronous release during the train (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: Prolonged calcium influx during optogenetic stimulation may have raised residual calcium levels and modulated baseline vesicle replenishment.
source: Prolonged calcium influx during optogenetic stimulation may have thus raised residual calcium levels and modulated baseline vesicle replenishment.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed slow kinetics of optically-evoked EPSCs.

claim: Optically-evoked IPSCs have normal kinetics.
source: Additionally, the results are matched at inhibitory synapses with normal baseline replenishment dynamics, since optically-evoked IPSCs have normal kinetics (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data from mixed hippocampal cultures.

claim: The effect of Arpc3 deletion on synaptic vesicle replenishment may be caused by an increased action potential width or increased release probability during each stimulation.
source: Because of this, it is possible that the effect of Arpc3 deletion on synaptic vesicle replenishment, as seen through increased current amplitudes at the end of the 20 Hz train, was actually caused by an increased action potential width or increased release probability during each stimulation.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about alternative explanations for the observed effects of Arpc3 deletion.

claim: The expected prolonged calcium influx in Arpc3 KO neurons may have raised residual calcium levels, which is known to accelerate synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: The expected prolonged calcium influx in KO neurons may have raised residual calcium levels, which is known to accelerate synaptic vesicle replenishment (Dittman and Regehr, 1998; Junge et al., 2004; Lipstein et al., 2013; Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Stevens and Wesseling, 1998; Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed increase in action potential width in Arpc3 KO neurons and cites previous work on calcium-dependent vesicle replenishment.

claim: The experiments using Arpc3 deletion cannot distinguish whether or not Rac1 and Arp2/3 function in the same pathway to negatively regulate synaptic vesicle replenishment.
source: Thus, this set of experiments cannot distinguish whether or not Rac1 and Arp2/3 function in the same pathway to negatively regulate synaptic vesicle replenishment.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgement of the limitations of the Arpc3 deletion experiments due to the confounding effect on action potential width.

claim: W56-Synapsin (or the scrambled control) was delivered to cultured hippocampal neurons after synaptic maturation.
source: After synaptic maturation, we delivered W56-Synapsin (or the scrambled control) to cultured hippocampal neurons and then recorded electrically evoked responses using more traditional methods.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: Electrical stimulation activated neurons within a ~700 μm radius around the electrode.
source: As before, using CaMPARI2, we calculated that electrical stimulation activated neurons within a ~700 μm radius around the electrode (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on CaMPARI2 imaging data.

claim: For a given target neuron in the W56 experiments, recorded responses were from the activation of ~13 presynaptic excitatory neurons or ~11 presynaptic inhibitory neurons.
source: We estimated that for a given target neuron, recorded responses were from the activation of ~13 presynaptic excitatory neurons or ~11 presynaptic inhibitory neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using CaMPARI2 data and previously reported connection probabilities.

claim: It is possible that vesicle replenishment may have reached the upper limit from the loss of Arp2/3 alone, with no additional vesicles whose replenishment could be increased upon Rac1 inhibition.
source: However, it is still possible that vesicle replenishment may have reached the upper limit from the loss of Arp2/3 alone, with no additional vesicles whose replenishment could be increased upon Rac1 inhibition.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgement of an alternative explanation for the occlusion observed in the Arpc3 KO + W56 experiments.

claim: The measurable time course of action potential-coupled Rac1 activation (on the order of minutes) is slower than the effects of Rac1 activity manipulation on short-term depression (on the order of seconds).
source: However, the measurable time course of action potential-coupled Rac1 activation (on the order of minutes) is slower than the effects of Rac1 activity manipulation on short-term depression (on the order of seconds).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the 2pFLIM data showing the time course of Rac1 activation and the electrophysiology data showing the time course of short-term depression.

claim: Due to the small size of presynaptic terminals, the time resolution of 2pFLIM was limited to ten seconds per frame.
source: Unfortunately, due to the small size of presynaptic terminals, our time resolution was limited to ten seconds per frame in order to capture enough photons for 2pFLIM.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgement of a technical limitation of the 2pFLIM experiments.

claim: The time resolution limit of 2pFLIM did not allow imaging of Rac1 activity during the short HFS trains that cause short-term depression.
source: This resolution limit did not allow us to image Rac1 activity during the short HFS trains that cause short-term depression.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgement of a limitation of the 2pFLIM experiments.

claim: The data are the first to suggest that Rac1 is activated by action potentials in presynaptic terminals.
source: Despite this limitation, our data are the first we know of to suggest that Rac1 is activated by action potentials in presynaptic terminals.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the 2pFLIM data showing Rac1 activation in response to electrical stimulation.

claim: The Rac1-Arp2/3 pathway is a common regulator of plasticity at both sides of the synapse.
source: The Rac1-Arp2/3 pathway is a common regulator of plasticity at both sides of the synapse, and many other signaling pathways that are thought to be confined to postsynaptic sites may also be engaged presynaptically.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings showing Rac1-Arp2/3 function at both pre- and postsynaptic sites.

claim: The experimental strategies developed in this study open numerous avenues of future research and bring into focus the exquisite, complex signaling that occurs in presynaptic terminals.
source: The experimental strategies and resources that we developed here open numerous avenues of future research, and bring into focus the exquisite, complex signaling that occurs in presynaptic terminals.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the broader impact of the study.

claim: The Synapsin iBioID approach led to the mass spectrometry-based identification of 200 proteins within mature presynaptic terminals of the hippocampus and cortex.
source: Similar to our previous work isolating the proteomes of inhibitory postsynapses (Uezu et al., 2016), dendritic filopodia (Spence et al., 2019), and perisynaptic astrocytic processes (Takano et al., 2020), this approach led to the mass spectrometry-based identification of 200 proteins within mature presynaptic terminals of the hippocampus and cortex.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by the mass spectrometry data and cites previous work using similar approaches.

claim: Rac1 and Arp2/3 have established roles at the postsynapse.
source: While Rac1 and Arp2/3 have established roles at the postsynapse (Hedrick and Yasuda, 2017; Kim et al., 2013; Spence et al., 2016; Tolias et al., 2011), here we discovered that Rac1 and Arp2/3 are also closely associated with presynaptic vesicle membranes in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and cites previous work.

claim: Rac1-Arp2/3 signaling negatively regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment and can bidirectionally alter STD.
source: We developed genetic, optogenetic, and electrophysiological strategies to specifically isolate presynaptic effects and demonstrated that Rac1-Arp2/3 signaling negatively regulates synaptic vesicle replenishment and can bidirectionally alter STD.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results of the genetic, optogenetic, and electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Rac1 activation is coupled to action potential trains via voltage-gated calcium influx.
source: By imaging a Rac1 activity sensor (Hedrick et al., 2016) in presynaptic terminals, we also found that Rac1 activation is coupled to action potential trains via voltage-gated calcium influx.
evidence: The claim is supported by the 2pFLIM data showing Rac1 activation in response to electrical stimulation that is blocked by TTX and Cd2+.

claim: Rac1 and branched actin have an important, previously uncharacterized presynaptic role in sculpting short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, Rac1 and branched actin have an important, previously uncharacterized presynaptic role in sculpting short-term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined results of the study.

claim: The results define a new activity-dependent signaling mechanism that contributes to STD and is conserved across cell types.
source: These results define a new activity-dependent signaling mechanism that contributes to STD and is conserved across cell types.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined results showing similar effects at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.

claim: The findings challenge the prevailing view that the Rac1-Arp2/3 pathway functions largely at excitatory postsynapses.
source: This also challenges the prevailing view that the Rac1-Arp2/3 pathway functions largely at excitatory postsynapses, prompting re-evaluation of its mechanism in neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings showing Rac1-Arp2/3 function at presynaptic terminals.
